content: The text of the manuscript is more effectively scrutinized by reviewers for plagiarism or self-plagiarism of prose than for fraudulent data. While self-plagiarism is more common than plagiarism, journals and employers often do not penalize authors for it. However, self-plagiarism violates the policies of most peer-reviewed journals, which typically require the submission of only unpublished material. A related form of professional misconduct involves reviewers exploiting unpublished information from manuscripts or grant applications for personal or professional gain. The frequency of such incidents is unknown, but the United States Office of Research Integrity has sanctioned reviewers caught engaging in this behavior. Authors can defend against this misconduct by pre-publishing their work as a preprint or technical report on public platforms like arXiv, which can later be used to establish priority. Open Peer Review Traditional anonymous peer review has been criticized for lacking accountability, enabling reviewer abuse, and being prone to bias and inconsistency. In response, alternative peer review systems with varying degrees of openness have been proposed. For example, in 1996, the Journal of Interactive Media in Education adopted open peer review, where reviewers' names are disclosed, making them accountable for their reviews while also acknowledging their contributions. Authors are allowed to respond, and other researchers can comment before publication. In 1999, the open-access Journal of Medical Internet Research began publishing reviewers' names at the end of each article. Similarly, the British Medical Journal (BMJ) transitioned to an open peer review system in 1999, revealing reviewers' identities to authors but not to readers. In 2000, the open-access BMC series by BioMed Central also adopted open peer review, publishing reviewers' names and making peer review reports available online as part of the pre-publication history. Other journals, such as those in the BMJ group and PLoS Medicine, offer optional open peer review. The impact of open peer review on the quality, tone, and time spent on reviews is mixed. However, it appears that under open peer review, more invited reviewers decline to participate. In 2006, Nature experimented with parallel open peer review, allowing some articles to undergo both anonymous and open public review. The results were underwhelming, with only 5% of authors agreeing to participate and only 54% of those articles receiving comments. Editors speculated that researchers were too busy or reluctant to reveal their identities, and the simultaneous anonymous review process may have influenced participation. In 2006, UK academics launched the online journal Philica, which addresses many issues of traditional peer review. Unlike conventional journals, all submitted articles are published immediately, and the review process occurs afterward. Reviews remain anonymous, but any researcher can review an article. Reviews are displayed at the end of each article, providing readers with criticism or guidance rather than determining publication. This system prevents reviewers from suppressing ideas they disagree with, and readers can easily identify popular or controversial work. Dynamic and Self-Organizing Peer Review A similar approach is used by the dynamic peer review site Naboj.org, where the review system is modeled on platforms like Amazon. Users can evaluate both the reviews and the articles, potentially leading to a higher-quality review process with sufficient participation. In February 2006, the journal Biology Direct was launched by Eugene Koonin, Laura Landweber, and David Lipman as another alternative to traditional peer review. Authors must secure three editorial board members to review or solicit external reviews for their article to be published. Unlike Philica, reviews are not anonymous, and no article is published without being reviewed. Authors can withdraw, revise, or publish their article despite critical comments, with all reviews and reviewers' names visible to readers. Open Peer Commentary An extension of peer review beyond publication is open peer commentary, where expert commentaries are solicited on published articles, and authors are encouraged to respond. The BMJ's Rapid Responses allow ongoing debate and criticism after publication. By 2005, stricter criteria for accepting Rapid Responses were enforced to filter out irrelevant contributions. Peer Review of Policy Peer review is also used to improve government policy. The European Union employs it in the Open Method of Coordination for policies in employment and social inclusion. Since 1999, peer review programs in active labor market policy and social inclusion have facilitated meetings where a host country presents a policy or initiative for examination by other countries and relevant European-level NGOs.
